domanda: Contoso plans to use object replication to asynchronously copy block blobs from a general-purpose v2 storage account named storageeast to a general-purpose v2 storage account named storagewest. Before the replication policy can be created, which storage features must be enabled?
opzione_a: Change feed on both the source and destination accounts, and blob versioning on the source account only.
opzione_b: Blob versioning on both the source and destination accounts, and change feed on the source account.
opzione_c: Blob versioning on the source account only, and blob soft delete on the destination account.
opzione_d: Point-in-time restore on the source account, and change feed on the destination account.
spiegazione: Correct: Object replication has exactly two feature prerequisites. Blob versioning must be enabled on BOTH the source and the destination account, and change feed must be enabled on the SOURCE account. Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed to discover write and delete operations, and versioning is what allows the current version and any previous versions to be replicated. Option A inverts the requirement: change feed is needed only on the source, not on both, and versioning on the source alone is not sufficient. Option C is wrong because versioning is required on both accounts, and blob soft delete is not a prerequisite for object replication at all. Option D is wrong because point-in-time restore is a separate data-protection feature that is not required by object replication, and change feed is required on the source rather than the destination.
tags: object replication, blob versioning, change feed, blob storage, prerequisites

domanda: An object replication policy is active between a source container named archive-src and a destination container named archive-dst. A developer uses the Azure portal to upload a new blob directly into archive-dst. What is the result?
opzione_a: The upload succeeds, and the blob is replicated back to the source container on the next replication cycle.
opzione_b: The upload succeeds, but the blob is deleted the next time the replication policy runs.
opzione_c: The upload fails with error code 409 (Conflict).
opzione_d: The upload fails with error code 403 (Forbidden).
spiegazione: Correct: After a replication policy is created, write operations to the destination container are not permitted, and any attempt to write fails with error code 409 (Conflict). To write to the destination container you must first disable replication, either by deleting the rule for that container or by removing the entire replication policy. Read and delete operations against the destination container are still permitted while the policy is active. Option A is wrong because object replication is strictly one-way from source to destination; there is no write-back path. Option B is wrong because the write never succeeds in the first place, so there is nothing for a later cycle to remove. Option D is wrong because 403 (Forbidden) is the error returned in a different scenario, for example when a customer-managed key has been revoked or an encryption scope has been disabled, not when writing to a replication destination.
tags: object replication, destination container, 409 conflict, replication rules, blob storage

domanda: You are designing an object replication topology for block blob data. Which of the following statements about object replication are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The source and destination storage accounts can reside in different regions and in different subscriptions.
opzione_b: A single source account can replicate to a maximum of two destination accounts, with one policy per destination account.
opzione_c: Object replication copies block blobs, append blobs, and page blobs.
opzione_d: Object replication is supported for storage accounts that have a hierarchical namespace enabled.
opzione_e: Snapshots of a blob in the source account are not replicated to the destination account.
spiegazione: Correct: (A) The source and destination accounts may be in the same region or in different regions, and in the same subscription or in different subscriptions; they may even reside in different Microsoft Entra tenants if cross-tenant replication is allowed. (B) A source account can replicate to no more than two destination accounts, with one policy for each destination, and an account can likewise serve as the destination for no more than two replication policies. (E) Object replication does not support blob snapshots, so any snapshots on a source blob are not replicated. Incorrect: (C) Object replication supports block blobs only; append blobs and page blobs are not supported. (D) Object replication is not yet supported in accounts that have a hierarchical namespace enabled, and blobs uploaded through Data Lake Storage APIs are not replicated.
tags: object replication, replication policies, block blobs, hierarchical namespace, snapshots

domanda: An administrator opens the Object replication blade of a general-purpose v2 storage account and selects Create replication rules to replicate data to a second general-purpose v2 account. Select the correct value for each statement about the default object replication behaviour.
opzione_a: Feature that must be enabled on the source account but not on the destination account: [Blob versioning | Change feed | Blob soft delete]
opzione_b: Default copy scope applied to a new replication rule: [Only new objects | Everything | Custom]
opzione_c: Blob types that object replication copies: [Block blobs only | Block and append blobs | Block append and page blobs]
opzione_d: Maximum number of destination accounts for a single source account: [1 | 2 | 10]
risposta_corretta: Change feed,Only new objects,Block blobs only,2
spiegazione: Change feed: change feed must be enabled on the source account only, because Azure Storage periodically inspects the source account's change feed to find operations to replicate. Blob versioning is required on both accounts, and blob soft delete is not a prerequisite, so neither is the correct answer for a source-only requirement. Only new objects: after you create a replication rule, preexisting blobs are ignored and only new block blobs added after the rule is created are copied by default. Everything and Custom are valid copy scope choices you can select by using the change link, but they are not the default. Block blobs only: object replication supports block blobs only; append blobs and page blobs are not supported. 2: a source account can replicate to no more than two destination accounts, with one policy per destination account, so 1 understates and 10 overstates the documented limit.
tags: object replication, copy scope, change feed, block blobs, azure portal

domanda:
Fabrikam has two general-purpose v2 storage accounts: storage1 in East US (subscription A) and storage2 in West Europe (subscription B). Both accounts belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Blob versioning is enabled on both accounts and change feed is enabled on storage1. An object replication policy replicates one container pair from storage1 to storage2, and the copy scope of the rule is left at its default value. The source container already contained 500 block blobs when the policy was created.

Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. The 500 block blobs that existed in the source container before the policy was created are replicated to the destination container.
2. You can disable blob versioning on storage1 while the replication policy is still in effect.
3. If a replicated blob in the source container is later moved to the archive tier, object replication of that blob fails.
opzione_a: The 500 block blobs that existed in the source container before the policy was created are replicated to the destination container.
opzione_b: You can disable blob versioning on storage1 while the replication policy is still in effect.
opzione_c: If a replicated blob in the source container is later moved to the archive tier, object replication of that blob fails.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: the default copy scope copies only new objects. After a replication rule is created, preexisting blobs are ignored and only new block blobs added after the rule was created are copied. To include the 500 existing blobs, the rule would have to be configured to copy everything, or to use a custom copy scope with a minimum creation time that predates them. Statement 2 - No: if a storage account has object replication policies in effect, you cannot disable blob versioning for that account. You must delete any object replication policies on the account before you can disable versioning. Statement 3 - Yes: object replication is supported when the source and destination accounts are in any online tier (hot, cool, or cold) and the tiers may differ, but object replication fails if a blob in either the source or the destination account is moved to the archive tier. Rehydrating an archived blob does not by itself trigger replication; replication is triggered only when the blob data is updated again after rehydration.
tags: object replication, copy scope, blob versioning, archive tier, troubleshooting

domanda: An object replication policy replicates block blobs from a source container to a destination container. Both storage accounts are general-purpose v2 accounts encrypted with customer-managed keys, and both accounts are online in the hot tier. Most blobs replicate successfully, but a subset of blobs consistently reports a replication status of failure in the source account. Investigation shows that a line-of-business application writes exactly that subset of blobs by supplying an encryption key on each Put Blob request. What is the most likely cause of the failures?
opzione_a: The destination account uses customer-managed keys, which are not supported by object replication.
opzione_b: Blobs in the source account that are encrypted with a customer-provided key cannot be replicated by object replication.
opzione_c: The change feed retention period on the source account expired before the blobs could be replicated.
opzione_d: Blob versioning was never enabled on the destination account, so those blobs have no version to replicate.
spiegazione: Correct: Supplying an encryption key on the request is the customer-provided key (CPK) scenario. Object replication is not supported for blobs in the source account that are encrypted with a customer-provided key, and the documentation lists CPK-encrypted source blobs as an explicit cause of replication failure. Option A is wrong because object replication is fully supported for accounts encrypted with either Microsoft-managed keys or customer-managed keys; only customer-provided keys break it, and the similarity of the names is the trap here. Option C is wrong because change feed retention is not a documented cause of replication failure, and it would not selectively affect only the blobs written by one application. Option D is wrong because blob versioning is a hard prerequisite on both the source and the destination account: without it the replication policy could not have been created at all, and no blobs would replicate rather than just a subset.
tags: object replication, customer-provided key, replication status, troubleshooting, encryption

domanda: You must configure object replication between two existing general-purpose v2 storage accounts by using the Az.Storage PowerShell module. Neither account currently has any containers, blob versioning, or change feed configured. Place the four actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Create the replication policy on the destination account by calling Set-AzStorageObjectReplicationPolicy with a policy ID of default.
opzione_b: Enable blob versioning on both accounts and enable change feed on the source account by calling Update-AzStorageBlobServiceProperty.
opzione_c: Create the same replication policy on the source account by using the policy ID returned from the destination account.
opzione_d: Create the source and destination containers by calling New-AzStorageContainer.
spiegazione: The documented PowerShell sequence is: (1) B - enable the prerequisites first, because blob versioning is required on both the source and the destination account and change feed is required on the source account before a policy can be created. (2) D - create the source and destination containers, because both containers must already exist before they can be named in a replication rule. (3) A - create the replication policy on the destination account, setting the policy ID to the string value default so that Azure Storage generates the real policy ID and the rule IDs for you. (4) C - create the same policy on the source account using the policy ID that was returned for the destination account. The policy ID on the source and destination accounts must be identical for replication to take place, which is why the destination must be configured first. Note that this ordering applies to PowerShell, Azure CLI, and the resource provider APIs. In the Azure portal you configure the policy only on the source account, and the portal automatically creates the matching policy on the destination account for you.
tags: object replication, az powershell, policy id, replication policy, configuration order

domanda: A security auditor asks you to describe how data at rest is protected in a general-purpose v2 storage account that was created five minutes ago and has not been modified since. Which statement is accurate?
opzione_a: Data is automatically encrypted with 256-bit AES encryption, and Azure Storage encryption cannot be disabled.
opzione_b: Data is encrypted only after an administrator turns on Azure Storage Service Encryption from the Encryption blade of the account.
opzione_c: Data is encrypted with 128-bit AES encryption by default, and you can upgrade the account to 256-bit AES encryption.
opzione_d: Only blob and file data is encrypted by default; queue and table data must be protected by using client-side encryption.
spiegazione: Correct: Azure Storage uses service-side encryption to automatically encrypt data when it is persisted to the cloud. Data is encrypted and decrypted transparently using 256-bit AES encryption, it is FIPS 140-2 compliant, encryption is enabled for all storage accounts, and Azure Storage encryption cannot be disabled. There is no additional cost. Option B is wrong because encryption is on by default and there is no switch to enable or disable it; the Encryption blade lets you choose the key management model (Microsoft-managed versus customer-managed keys), not whether encryption occurs. Option C is wrong because the cipher strength is 256-bit AES from the start and is not configurable. Option D is wrong because all Azure Storage resources are encrypted, including blobs, disks, files, queues, and tables, and all object metadata is encrypted as well; client-side encryption is an optional additional capability, not a requirement for queues and tables.
tags: storage encryption, encryption at rest, aes-256, microsoft-managed keys, sse

domanda: Your compliance team requires that an existing general-purpose v2 storage account be encrypted with a customer-managed key that your organization stores in Azure Key Vault. Which configuration must be in place on the key vault before you can enable customer-managed keys on the storage account?
opzione_a: Soft delete and purge protection must both be enabled on the key vault.
opzione_b: The key vault must use the vault access policy permission model rather than Azure RBAC.
opzione_c: The key vault must reside in the same region and the same subscription as the storage account.
opzione_d: The key vault must contain an elliptic curve (EC) key of at least 256 bits.
spiegazione: Correct: The key vault or managed HSM that stores the customer-managed key must have both soft delete and purge protection enabled. This prevents a deleted or purged key from permanently orphaning the data that its wrapped account encryption key protects. Option B is wrong because the documented requirement is simply that the managed identity be granted the get, wrapKey, and unwrapKey permissions on the key; the permission model itself is not dictated. Option C is wrong because the documentation explicitly states that the storage account and the key vault or managed HSM can be in different Microsoft Entra tenants, regions, and subscriptions. Option D is wrong because Azure Storage encryption supports RSA and RSA-HSM keys of sizes 2048, 3072, and 4096 only; elliptic curve keys are not supported for storage account encryption.
tags: customer-managed keys, azure key vault, soft delete, purge protection, storage encryption

domanda: You are preparing to protect a storage account with a customer-managed key held in an Azure key vault. Select the correct value for each requirement.
opzione_a: Key type and key sizes supported for storage account encryption: [RSA 2048/3072/4096 | EC-P256/EC-P384 | AES-128/AES-256]
opzione_b: Minimum key permissions the managed identity needs on the key: [get + wrapKey + unwrapKey | get + list + create | sign + verify + decrypt]
opzione_c: Managed identity type required when you configure customer-managed keys at the time you create the storage account: [System-assigned | User-assigned | Either type]
opzione_d: Configuration that makes Azure Storage pick up new key versions automatically: [Omit the key version | Specify the full key version URI | Assign the Key Vault Contributor role]
risposta_corretta: RSA 2048/3072/4096,get + wrapKey + unwrapKey,User-assigned,Omit the key version
spiegazione: RSA 2048/3072/4096: Azure Storage encryption supports RSA and RSA-HSM keys of sizes 2048, 3072, and 4096. EC keys are not supported, and AES is the symmetric algorithm used for the data itself rather than a key type you can place in the vault for this purpose. get + wrapKey + unwrapKey: the managed identity associated with the storage account must have at minimum the wrapKey, unwrapKey, and get permissions, because Azure Storage wraps the account encryption key with the customer-managed key and must unwrap it for read and write operations. get + list + create and sign + verify + decrypt are real Key Vault key permissions but they are not the ones required here. User-assigned: when you configure customer-managed keys at the time that you create a storage account, you must use a user-assigned managed identity, because a system-assigned identity does not exist until the account has been created and therefore cannot be granted key permissions in advance. Only when you configure customer-managed keys on an existing storage account can you use either a user-assigned or a system-assigned managed identity. Omit the key version: to automatically update to a new key version, omit the key version when you enable encryption with customer-managed keys. Azure Storage then checks the key vault daily for a new version and uses the latest one. Specifying the full key version URI pins the account to that version and forces manual updates, and a Key Vault rotation policy rotates the key in the vault but does not by itself change how the storage account references the key.
tags: customer-managed keys, managed identity, key rotation, key vault, storage encryption

domanda: A regulator requires that all existing and future data in a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 be encrypted twice, once at the service level and once at the infrastructure level, with two different algorithms and two different keys. The account was created 18 months ago without infrastructure encryption and currently holds 4 TB of blob data. What should you do?
opzione_a: On the Encryption blade of storage1, set Enable infrastructure encryption to Enabled.
opzione_b: Create a new general-purpose v2 storage account with infrastructure encryption enabled and migrate the data from storage1 to the new account.
opzione_c: Configure a customer-managed key for storage1 and add a second key in the key vault to act as the infrastructure-level key.
opzione_d: Create an encryption scope on storage1 with infrastructure encryption enabled and apply it to the existing containers.
spiegazione: Correct: To enable infrastructure encryption for a storage account, you must configure the account to use infrastructure encryption at the time that you create the account. Infrastructure encryption cannot be enabled or disabled after the account has been created, so the only way to satisfy the requirement for the existing 4 TB is to create a new account (general-purpose v2, premium block blob, premium page blob, or premium file shares) with infrastructure encryption enabled and migrate the data. Option A is wrong because the portal exposes Enable infrastructure encryption on the Encryption tab only while creating the account; on an existing account the Encryption blade lets you verify the setting but not change it. Option C is wrong because customer-managed keys apply to service-level encryption only. Infrastructure-level encryption always relies on Microsoft-managed keys and always uses a separate key, so you cannot supply your own second key. Option D is wrong on two counts: a default encryption scope must be specified for a container at the time the container is created, so it cannot be applied to existing containers, and even if new containers were created, applying a scope does not re-encrypt the 4 TB of data that already exists.
tags: infrastructure encryption, double encryption, storage encryption, account creation, compliance

domanda: A multitenant SaaS application stores each customer's blobs in the same storage account and uses encryption scopes to create secure boundaries between them. Which statements about encryption scopes are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: An encryption scope can be protected with either a Microsoft-managed key or a customer-managed key stored in Azure Key Vault.
opzione_b: The infrastructure encryption setting for an encryption scope cannot be changed after the scope is created.
opzione_c: A default encryption scope can be assigned to a container at any time after the container has been created.
opzione_d: An encryption scope can be deleted from the storage account when it is no longer needed.
opzione_e: If infrastructure encryption is enabled at the account level, every encryption scope created in that account automatically uses infrastructure encryption.
spiegazione: Correct: (A) When you define an encryption scope you can specify whether it is protected with a Microsoft-managed key or with a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault, and different scopes in the same account can use different key types. You can also switch a scope between the two key types at any time. (B) The infrastructure encryption setting for an encryption scope cannot be changed after the scope is created; if the account does not already have infrastructure encryption, you can only opt in for a scope at the time you create that scope. (E) If infrastructure encryption is enabled for an account, then any encryption scope created on that account automatically uses infrastructure encryption. Incorrect: (C) A default encryption scope must be specified for a container at the time that the container is created; it cannot be added to an existing container afterwards. (D) It is not possible to delete an encryption scope. You can only disable it, after which read and write operations that use the scope fail with HTTP 403 (Forbidden). Note also that an enabled scope is billed for a minimum of 30 days.
tags: encryption scopes, infrastructure encryption, customer-managed keys, blob storage, multitenant

domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named storage2 is configured to use a customer-managed key stored in a key vault named kv1. The key vault and the storage account are in the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Access to the key is authorized through the system-assigned managed identity of storage2, and the customer-managed key configuration was saved without specifying a key version. The storage account was created by using the Azure portal with default settings and hosts blob, file, queue, and table data.

Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. If an administrator disables the key in kv1, client requests to read blob data from storage2 fail with error code 403 (Forbidden).
2. Data stored in the Queue and Table services of storage2 is automatically protected by the customer-managed key.
3. After a new version of the key is created in kv1, you must manually update storage2 to reference the new key version URI.
opzione_a: If an administrator disables the key in kv1, client requests to read blob data from storage2 fail with error code 403 (Forbidden).
opzione_b: Data stored in the Queue and Table services of storage2 is automatically protected by the customer-managed key.
opzione_c: After a new version of the key is created in kv1, you must manually update storage2 to reference the new key version URI.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: disabling the key in the key vault is the documented way to revoke access to a storage account that uses customer-managed keys. After the key has been disabled, clients cannot call operations that read from or write to a resource or its metadata, and those operations fail with error code 403 (Forbidden) for all users, including Get Blob. Restoring access to the key restores the operations. Statement 2 - No: data stored in Queue and Table storage is not automatically protected by a customer-managed key when customer-managed keys are enabled for the storage account. Queue and table protection can only be configured at the time that you create the storage account, which was not done here. By contrast, data in Blob storage and Azure Files is always protected by the customer-managed key once it is configured for the account. Statement 3 - No: because the key version was omitted when customer-managed keys were configured, Azure Storage checks the key vault daily for a new version of the key and automatically uses the latest version. Manual updating of the key version URI is required only when a specific key version was explicitly pinned in the configuration. Because the check happens only once per day, you should wait 24 hours after rotating a key before disabling the older version.
tags: customer-managed keys, key revocation, queues and tables, key version, storage encryption

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: A nightly unattended job on a Windows server must make a blob container an exact mirror of the local folder C:\\data. Files that are added or changed locally must be uploaded, and blobs whose corresponding local files were deleted must be removed from the container. The job runs from a scheduled task, so no interactive prompt can be answered. Which AzCopy v10 command should you run?
spiegazione: Correct: The sync command replicates the source location to the destination location, comparing file names and last modified timestamps by default. Setting the --delete-destination flag to true makes AzCopy delete files in the destination that no longer exist in the source, and it does so without providing a prompt, which is what an unattended scheduled task requires. Option B is wrong because the prompt value makes AzCopy ask for confirmation before each deletion, which will stall a job that has no interactive console. Option C is wrong because the copy command never removes objects from the destination; --overwrite=ifSourceNewer only controls whether an existing destination object is replaced, so blobs for deleted local files would remain. (Microsoft does recommend copy with --overwrite=ifSourceNewer over sync when you do not need deletions, because copy consumes less memory and incurs less billing cost.) Option D is wrong because --delete-destination is an option of the sync command, not of the copy command. As a safeguard, enable blob soft delete before you use --delete-destination=true or prompt.
tags: azcopy, azcopy sync, delete-destination, blob storage, data transfer

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: A user is assigned the Owner role scoped to a storage account named contoso. The user runs azcopy login, signs in successfully with their Microsoft Entra ID credentials, and then runs azcopy copy to upload files to a blob container in contoso. The upload fails with an authorization error. You must resolve the failure while continuing to use Microsoft Entra ID authorization. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the Storage Blob Data Contributor role to the user, scoped to the storage account.
opzione_b: Assign the Storage Account Contributor role to the user, scoped to the storage account.
opzione_c: Assign the Reader role to the user, scoped to the subscription that contains the storage account.
opzione_d: Regenerate key1 for the storage account and rerun azcopy login.
spiegazione: Correct: As the documentation states, an owner of a storage account is not automatically assigned permissions to access the data. Owner is a control-plane (Azure Resource Manager) role; it does not grant data-plane access when AzCopy presents a Microsoft Entra ID OAuth token. For upload operations against Blob Storage the user needs Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. (Role assignments can take up to five minutes to propagate.) Option B is wrong because Storage Account Contributor is likewise a control-plane role that manages the account resource but grants no access to blob data over Microsoft Entra ID. Option C is wrong because Reader is a control-plane role and grants no data access whatsoever, and it is even weaker than the Owner role the user already holds. Option D is wrong because regenerating an account key is irrelevant to Microsoft Entra ID authorization; account keys are a different authorization mechanism, and azcopy login obtains an OAuth token that has nothing to do with the account keys.
tags: azcopy, microsoft entra id, storage blob data contributor, rbac, data plane

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: Your team uses AzCopy v10 for scripted transfers and Azure Storage Explorer for ad hoc browsing of blob data. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Authorization credentials that AzCopy accepts for the storage service: [Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token | Storage account key or a SAS token | Microsoft Entra ID or a storage account key]
opzione_b: Least privileged built-in role for downloading blobs with AzCopy by using a user identity: [Storage Blob Data Reader | Reader | Storage Account Contributor]
opzione_c: Values that the azcopy sync command compares by default: [File names and last modified timestamps | MD5 hashes | File sizes only]
opzione_d: Storage Explorer method for attaching a single blob container when you have data-layer access but no management-layer access: [Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID | Account name and key | Local storage emulator]
risposta_corretta: Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token,Storage Blob Data Reader,File names and last modified timestamps,Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token: AzCopy accepts credentials either by using Microsoft Entra ID (user identity, managed identity, or service principal) or by appending a SAS token to each source or destination URL. AzCopy does not take a storage account key, which rules out the two options that include one. Storage Blob Data Reader: for download operations against Blob Storage the documented role is Storage Blob Data Reader; upload operations require Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. Reader and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles that do not grant access to blob data. File names and last modified timestamps: by default the sync command compares file names and last modified timestamps. You can override that behaviour to use MD5 hashes instead by using the --compare-hash flag, so MD5 hashes is the opt-in behaviour rather than the default. Because last modified times are critical when --compare-hash is not used, the machine running sync should have an accurate system clock. Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID: Microsoft Entra ID is the preferred option if you have data layer access to your resource but no management layer access, and Storage Explorer supports it when attaching blob containers, Data Lake Storage containers and directories, and queues. Account name and key is not offered when attaching an individual blob container (it applies to attaching a whole storage account), and the local storage emulator connects to Azurite or the Azure Storage Emulator rather than to a real container.
tags: azcopy, azure storage explorer, sas token, microsoft entra id, azcopy sync
